extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in British constitutional history, law, and political theory (scholars, students, informed citizens)
extracted.subtask_description: An argumentative/historical analysis defending the primacy of hereditary succession in British constitutional practice and specifying when extraordinary deviations (revolutions, removals) are justified and how constitutional change should be constrained. The text articulates normative and practical standards for legitimacy, continuity, and remedies against abuse of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize principle from a special-case law
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is against all genuine principles of jurisprudence to draw a principle from a law made in a special case and regarding an individual person. Privilegium non transit in exemplum.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Revolution and the temporary deviation (King William) were special, exceptional measures of necessity; one must not derive a general constitutional principle (for example, that the people have a right to elect kings) from such isolated acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Revolution did not create a right to elect kings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution did not confer on the nation the right to choose its governors as a general rule; indeed the nation renounced any such elective right for itself and its posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Declaration of Right and subsequent statutes were framed to avoid recognizing an elective title; contemporary legislators deliberately avoided language that would make election the lawful title to the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of succession is essential to national unity and tranquillity
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature declared that 'on the preserving a certainty in the SUCCESSION thereof, the unity, peace, and tranquillity of this nation doth, under God, wholly depend.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A doubtful title to the crown resembles an election and threatens the unity, peace, and tranquillity of the state; legal certainty of succession is a constitutional value to be preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating precedents that resemble elective succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament avoided the appearance of choice at the Revolution and covered every circumstance tending to weaken hereditary rights with language and forms that emphasized continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constitutionally exceptional acts occur, legislatures should cloak them in continuity language (recognition, thanksgiving, incorporation of prerogatives) so as not to relax the hereditary principle or create a practicable precedent for future elective claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the moral competence of constituent bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain acts are morally or constitutionally beyond the competence of constituent parts (e.g., 'The House of Lords... is not morally competent to dissolve the House of Commons, no, nor even to dissolve itself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constituent organs must respect the public pact and cannot surrender or abdicate irrevocable portions of the constitution for the whole body; there are moral limits on what bodies may lawfully do to alter the constitutional order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency deviations must be confined and not decompose the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in extremity the change is to be confined to the peccant part only, and even then effected without a decomposition of the whole civil and political mass for the purpose of originating a new civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial or corrective acts taken in emergencies should be targeted, temporary, and avoid wholesale reconstruction; preserve the broader constitutional framework while addressing the defective element.

rubrics_metrics.name: A state must retain lawful means of change to ensure conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and institutional mechanisms for change are necessary to preserve the constitution; absence of any means of change risks losing the very parts one seeks to protect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession may be legislatively qualified but remains hereditary
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the crown was carried somewhat out of the old line, 'the new line was derived from the same stock'—it remained hereditary, even if qualified (e.g., by Protestantism in the Act of Settlement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament may modify modes or conditions (e.g., religious tests), but such modifications should preserve the core hereditary principle and continuity of descent rather than creating a fundamentally elective model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of sovereign requires grave, defined grounds rather than vague 'misconduct'
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Revolution they grounded James's virtual abdication on a design, confirmed by a multitude of illegal overt acts to subvert church, state and fundamental laws—more than mere 'misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposing or cashiering a sovereign should be based on serious, substantial, and demonstrable breaches (e.g., attempts to subvert the constitution), not on indeterminate notions of misconduct; the threshold for such an extraordinary measure must be high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional remedies are preferable to cashiering sovereigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature thought the Declaration of Right, constant parliamentary inspection, and the practical claim of impeachment infinitely better security than the reservation of a right to 'cashier their governors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured legal mechanisms (frequent parliaments, impeachment, statutory limits on pardons) to control abuse rather than relying on violent or extra-constitutional removal of a monarch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kings are sovereigns, not servants removable at pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although kings are for the general advantage they are not servants in the ordinary constitutional sense; 'the law... calls this high magistrate not our servant... but "our sovereign Lord the king".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate rhetorical formulations (king as 'servant of the people') with constitutional status; the king is not constitutionally liable to be treated like a removable servant and the constitution provides no servant-like process for his removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution is an extraordinary, last-resort response, governed by statesmanship not ordinary law
rubrics_metrics.description: The ceremony of cashiering kings can rarely be performed without force... The question of dethroning or 'cashiering kings' will always be an extraordinary question of state, and wholly out of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolution is to be contemplated only when the state's condition is desperate; judgment rests on dispositions, means, and probable consequences and should be left to those qualified to act in extremity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The right to 'form a government for ourselves' lacks precedent; prefer reform by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The very idea of the fabrication of a new government is enough to fill us with disgust and horror; all reformations made proceed upon reverence to antiquity and analogical precedent, authority, and example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wholesale invention of new constitutional forms; legitimate reform should be grounded in recorded precedent, analogical reasoning, and continuity with the constitution's historic pedigree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberties are to be asserted as inherited, positive, recorded rights rather than vague abstract 'rights of men'
rubrics_metrics.description: From Magna Charta to the Declaration of Right it has been the uniform policy to claim and assert our liberties as an entailed inheritance derived to us from our forefathers, and not as abstract principles 'as the rights of men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground constitutional claims in recorded charters, statutes, and historical pedigree (Magna Carta, Petition of Right) to secure stability and to avoid speculative, abstract formulations that could unsettle established inheritance of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish legal rules to limit ministerial impunity (e.g., limit pardons)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 12th and 13th of King William they provided 'that no pardon under the great seal of England should be pleadable to an impeachment by the Commons in parliament.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create statutory restraints (such as non-pleadability of royal pardons to impeachment) to ensure ministers remain accountable and to reduce the need for extra-constitutional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating liberties/government as inheritance promotes temperance and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: By considering liberties in the light of an inheritance, the spirit of freedom is tempered with an awful gravity; this idea prevents upstart insolence and gives institutions dignity, pedigree, and reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing institutions and liberties as transmitted from ancestors fosters respect, continuity, and moderation in exercise of liberty, helping to secure constitutional permanence and civic temperance.
